passage:
"It'll be sunny," Asif told his mother Kashish while she packed sandwiches. He drew a big smiling sun on a page and stuck it to the fridge.
In the morning, rain tapped at the window. Asif's face crumpled. "It's not sunny."
Kashish knelt beside him. "The park is wet. But I said we'd have a picnic, and we will."
She spread the checked cloth on the living-room floor. Asif set out the sandwiches in a row, then put on his sun hat. "It's still a picnic," he announced.
By noon the clouds thinned.

qa.q: What did Asif draw and stick to the fridge?
qa.a: Asif drew a big smiling sun and stuck it to the fridge.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he saw the rain?
qa.a: Asif felt disappointed and upset, because he had been sure it would be sunny.

qa.q: How did Kashish keep her promise when the plan changed?
qa.a: Kashish kept the promise of a picnic by spreading the cloth on the living-room floor, so Asif's trust in her stayed intact.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Asif's face crumpled at the rain?
qa.a: Probably concerned for Asif and determined to keep her promise, since she knelt beside him and said they would still have a picnic.

grounding: A child plans a picnic and is sure it will be sunny; early hope is trust that adults will provide a good future.

passage:
Kiran lay in bed with her yellow shoes beside the pillow.
"Papa, tomorrow's picnic by the lake will be sunny. I already know."
"How do you know?"
"Because I'm going to wear my hat. And I'll bring the ball, and we'll eat under the big tree."
"You've thought of everything."
"You'll come, Papa? You promised."
"I promised. I'll be home by four and we'll go straight there."
"Pinky promise?"
Harsha hooked his little finger around hers. "Pinky promise."
Kiran smiled and closed her eyes, already halfway into tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Kiran keep beside her pillow?
qa.a: Kiran kept her yellow shoes beside her pillow.

qa.q: What is Kiran feeling as she talks about tomorrow?
qa.a: Kiran is excited and trusting. She is certain of the sunny day and asks for a promise because she believes her papa will keep it.

qa.q: Why is Harsha's pinky promise important to Kiran's hope?
qa.a: It gives Kiran something she can rely on, that Papa will come home by four and take her. Her trust rests on adults doing what they say.

qa.q: What might Harsha be feeling as Kiran asks for a pinky promise?
qa.a: Harsha likely feels tender and responsible, since he answers seriously and hooks his finger round hers, aware that she is counting on him.

grounding: A child plans tomorrow's picnic and trusts an adult's promise; early hope is simple trust that adults will provide a good future.

passage: In their Lajpat Nagar flat, Zubin, five, packed his little bag for tomorrow's picnic: one ball, two biscuits, his toy giraffe. "It will be sunny," he told Dolma from next door. "Papa promised." Dolma looked at the grey sky. "What if it rains?" Zubin shook his head. "It won't." In the morning, it was raining. Zubin's lip trembled. Papa knelt down. "I promised a picnic, and we'll have one." He spread the mat on the balcony. They ate biscuits and watched the rain. Zubin giggled. "Tomorrow's picnic can be sunny."

qa.q: What did Zubin pack in his bag?
qa.a: One ball, two biscuits and his toy giraffe.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when he saw the rain?
qa.a: He was disappointed and near tears, his lip trembling.

qa.q: How did Papa protect Zubin's trust?
qa.a: He kept the promise in a new way, having the picnic on the balcony, so Zubin still felt he could rely on him.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had simply cancelled the picnic?
qa.a: Zubin might have felt let down, and his simple trust that good things will come could have been shaken.

grounding: Shows a young child sure that tomorrow's picnic will be sunny, and a parent keeping the promise so the child's trust stays safe.

passage:
"Didi, tomorrow the zoo will be sunny, na?" Mridul asked, bouncing on the bed.
"I hope so," said Bhavna, his big sister.
"It WILL be. Papa said. We'll see the tiger."
"Last time Papa said, he had to work," Bhavna said quietly.
Mridul stopped bouncing. "He did?"
"You cried all day, remember?"
Mridul's face crumpled. Papa came in. "What's wrong?"
"Are we REALLY going?"
Papa looked at Bhavna, then at Mridul. "I've told my office already. We're going. Rain or sun."
Mridul threw his arms round Papa's neck. "Then it will be sunny!"

qa.q: Which animal did Mridul want to see?
qa.a: The tiger.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when Bhavna reminded him about last time?
qa.a: He was worried and upset, his face crumpling as his certainty about tomorrow wobbled.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped rebuild Mridul's trust?
qa.a: He said clearly that he had already told his office and they were going, rain or sun.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Papa's promise?
qa.a: Bhavna remembers the cancelled trip, so she may be more cautious, hoping Papa keeps it this time.

grounding: Shows a young child who simply trusts tomorrow will be good, and how an earlier broken promise briefly shook that trust.

passage:
Nursery note, Thursday.
Himani (5) talked about tomorrow's park picnic all day. She told Uma, "It will be sunny and there will be swings and cake." When Uma said it might rain, Himani said firmly, "No. Ma'am promised." She drew a big yellow sun on every page.
Last month our farm trip was cancelled at the last minute, and Himani cried all morning. So after class I confirmed the park booking and planned an indoor picnic in the hall if it rains.
I told Himani, "Whatever the weather, we'll have our picnic." She beamed and added more rays.

qa.q: What did Himani draw on every page?
qa.a: A big yellow sun.

qa.q: What does Himani saying 'Ma'am promised' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt confident and trusting, sure that the adults would make tomorrow good.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She confirmed the booking and planned an indoor picnic, so the promise will be kept whatever the weather and Himani's trust isn't broken again.

qa.q: How might Uma feel about the picnic?
qa.a: Uma seems less sure, thinking it might rain, but will probably enjoy it too, since the teacher has a plan either way.

grounding: Shows a young child confidently trusting that tomorrow's picnic will be good, and a teacher protecting that trust after an earlier broken plan.

passage: Kalyani packed her own bag the night before: a steel tumbler, two groundnut laddoos and her cloth doll. "Tomorrow we go to the mango grove, and it will be sunny," she told the goat. In the morning the village sky was grey, and big drops tapped the tin roof. Kalyani's face crumpled. "You said!" Her mother, Ganga, knelt down. "I said picnic. Picnic we'll have." She spread the mat on the verandah and set out the laddoos. Kalyani ate, watching the rain. "Tomorrow the grove?" "If the sky lets us." Kalyani nodded, sure again.

qa.q: What did Kalyani pack in her bag?
qa.a: She packed a steel tumbler, two groundnut laddoos and her cloth doll.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when the rain came?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and let down 😔 Her face crumpled as she said, "You said!"

qa.q: What did Ganga do that kept Kalyani's trust?
qa.a: She kept the part she had promised by holding the picnic on the verandah, and was careful to say "If the sky lets us" about tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had simply said, "No picnic today"?
qa.a: Kalyani might feel the promise was broken and trust tomorrow's plans a little less.

grounding: Shows a young child sure that tomorrow's picnic will be sunny, and a parent keeping the promise so that simple hope stays safe.
